abstract: |
  The murderer at the door is Benjamin Constant's example, offered in 1797 to illustrate a theory on which the essence of a principle is not generality but fixity: a principle is a rule people can count on, as against the arbitrary. By that standard Constant's own resolution, that no one has a right to a truth that harms others, fails, for reasons he had himself given against duties keyed to consequences. But the pamphlet's next chapter contains a different key, the reciprocity of rights and duties between a people and an arbitrary power, and a neglected note of 1815 applies it to truthfulness: "when pretended laws demand the truth of us only to proscribe us, we do not owe them the truth." Keyed to the legitimacy and purpose of the demand rather than to harm, the later principle escapes the objections to the earlier one and agrees with Kant that the questioner is not wronged; but it does not escape judgement, as Constant came to admit. What remains between Constant and Kant is the premise Kant called Constant's fundamental error, that the duty of truthfulness is owed to those with a right to it.

# Constant's example {#sec-intro}

The example now called "the murderer at the door" is not Kant's. In the eighth chapter of *Des réactions politiques*, a pamphlet signed on 10 germinal year V (30 March 1797), Benjamin Constant wrote that "a German philosopher" goes so far as to claim "that towards assassins who asked you whether your friend, whom they are pursuing, has not taken refuge in your house, a lie would be a crime" [@Constant1797, 74].^[Translations from Constant and Kant are mine. After this note, @Constant1797 is cited by page alone; Kant is cited by volume and page of the Akademie edition [@KantAA].] Kant read the passage in Carl Friedrich Cramer's German translation, admitted in a note that he had said something of the kind (8:425), and replied in September in "On a Supposed Right to Lie from Love of Humanity". The reply became one of the most discussed short texts in moral philosophy, and Constant became its foil.

Constant's side has had less attention. The most thorough recent study, Jens Timmermann's, treats his proposal as a restatement of an "eighteenth-century commonplace", that a would-be murderer forfeits his right to the truth, and holds that Constant "is not talking about the state" [@Timmermann2025, 96 and n. 60]. Others have noticed that Constant does not present his restriction as an exception [@Zupancic1993, 179], that his definition of a principle differs from Kant's [@Loparic2006, 63–65], and that the example belongs to the politics of the Revolution [@Wood2011, citing @Holmes1984; @Troitsky2016; @Rousseliere2018].

I offer a reading of the exchange from Constant's side, in five steps. Constant offers the example to illustrate a theory on which a principle's essence is its *fixity*, and its point is protection against the arbitrary (@sec-principles). His 1797 resolution fails that theory, for reasons he had himself given against duties keyed to consequences (@sec-harm). The pamphlet's next chapter contains a different key, the reciprocity of rights and duties between a people and a power that has become arbitrary, and a note of 1815, so far as I know never connected with the exchange, applies it to truthfulness (@sec-pretended). That later key escapes the objections to the earlier one and agrees with Kant that the questioner is not wronged. But it does not escape judgement, as Constant came to admit, and it leaves untouched the premise Kant called Constant's fundamental error: that the duty of truthfulness is owed only to those with a right to it (@sec-remains).

# What a principle is {#sec-principles}

*Des réactions politiques* defends the republic of year III against the reactions that followed the Terror. Its seventh to ninth chapters defend principles against those who exaggerate them until they become inapplicable and those who conclude from the excesses that principles are useless; Burke is named for holding that axioms "metaphysically true" can be "politically false" (81). Constant's opponents charge men of principle with making "exceptions without number in favour of your own interests" (62), a charge he rejects; the mass of citizens, he observes, has no interest in "individual exceptions" and every interest in general principles being observed (64).

Chapter VIII, "Des principes", begins with a definition:

> A principle is the general result of a certain number of particular facts. Whenever the set of these facts undergoes some change, the principle that resulted from it is modified; but then this modification itself becomes a principle. (66)

Every combination of existences or events leads to a result, "and this result is always the same, whenever the combinations are the same". The result is general "only in relation to the combinations from which it results … only in a relative and not an absolute way" (66). There are universal principles, because some data are present in all combinations; to them must be added principles "resulting from each particular combination" (67). Those who call general principles inapplicable mean only that the intermediate principle a combination requires has not been found; "one of the links of the chain" is lost (67). Then:

> Secondary principles are just as immutable as first principles. Each interruption of the great chain has only one link to fill it. … Each circumstance calls only for the principle proper to it, for the essence of a principle is not to be general, nor applicable to many cases, but to be fixed; and this quality so far makes up its essence that all its utility resides in it. (67–68)

A principle's *generality* is its breadth. Its *fixity* has, in the pamphlet, three aspects that need to be kept apart. One is invariance: like combinations, like results (66). Another is reliance: in chapter IX, morality is "an assemblage of rules on which individuals must be able to count mutually in their social relations" (82), and political institutions "are only contracts", whose nature "is to set fixed limits" (84). The third, which the second requires, is that the principle can be applied without leaving the decision to whoever applies it. The arbitrary is "the absence of rules, of limits, of definitions, in a word the absence of all that is precise" (80), and if principles are abandoned "only circumstances remain, and each person is judge of the circumstances" (78).

Kant accepts the framework. He calls Constant's remark on inapplicable principles "well thought and at the same time correct" (8:427), restates his political example, on which the principle that no one is bound by laws he has not helped to make is applied in a large society through representation (72), as an axiom, a postulate and a problem (8:429), and concludes that intermediate principles may contain "the closer determination [*nähere Bestimmung*] of their application to cases", but "never exceptions" (8:430). The agreement is unsurprising if chapter VIII answers Kant's essay of 1793 on theory and practice, as Hinz has argued [@Timmermann2025, 43 n. 16]; there Kant had written that when theory is of little use in practice, "it was not the fault of the theory, but that there was not enough theory" (8:275). Both men demand principles without exceptions. They differ over what counts as one.

They differ also over judgement, though neither says so. What Constant took to be new was a method: an intermediate principle is found by *defining* the principle that seems inapplicable, "surveying its whole circumference", until we find "the link that unites it to another principle" (74–75). "It is an idea perhaps new, but which seems to me infinitely important, that every principle contains, either in itself or in its relation to another principle, its means of application" (77). Kant had insisted that between a rule and its application there must be an act of judgement for which rules cannot always be given, "because that would go on to infinity" (8:275). Constant's method tries to do without that act; "personal judgement has no role to play because the scope of one principle is limited by another" [@Timmermann2025, 94 n. 56]. That is the standard by which his resolution of the example should be judged.

# The 1797 key {#sec-harm}

Morality, Constant says, is "a science much more advanced than politics", because the need for it is daily and its direction "was not distorted by the personal interests of the depositaries or usurpers of power" (73). Yet its abstract principles, separated from their intermediate principles, would disorder social relations as badly as abstract political principles disorder civil ones. Then the example (74), introduced as a dilemma. The principle that telling the truth is a duty, taken in isolation, "is inapplicable. It would destroy society. But if you reject it, society will be no less destroyed, for all the foundations of morality will be overturned" (75). The way out is definition:

> Telling the truth is a duty. What is a duty? The idea of duty is inseparable from that of rights: a duty is what, in one being, corresponds to the rights of another. Where there are no rights, there are no duties. Telling the truth is therefore a duty only towards those who have a right to the truth. But no man has a right to a truth that harms others. (75–76)

"There, it seems to me, is the principle become applicable" (76). By defining it "we have found the precise modification of the principle of truth, which excludes all arbitrariness and all uncertainty" (76–77). By Constant's lights this is not an exception: when the facts change, "this modification itself becomes a principle" (66), as immutable as the duty it modifies.

What the modification is keyed to matters. It is keyed to harm. The clause does not say that those who would use the truth for a crime lose their right to it. It says that no one has a right to a truth "qui nuit à autrui", that harms someone other than the questioner. The assassins drop out of the principle's statement; what decides is the truth's effect on the friend. Timmermann registers this, glossing the clause as denying a right to the truth to those whose "knowing and acting on this truth will harm another", but describes the result in terms of forfeiture: "those who intend to do harm lose their right to be told the truth" [-@Timmermann2025, 100, 44]. That paraphrase, we shall see, fits a principle Constant came to later. The 1797 clause makes the case turn on consequences.

Constant had already said what is wrong with that. In December 1794, discussing Kant with Isabelle de Charrière, he sided with "absolute and independent duty" against duty that makes happiness its touchstone, because happiness "differs in the imagination of each individual": "Duty is thus ground to bits in accordance with [the preferences of] each individual head. What is more, a duty that turns into calculations of happiness is no longer a duty" [Timmermann's translation, @Timmermann2025, 44]. A duty keyed to harm is not keyed to happiness, but it shares the defect Constant names. Whether a truth harms others depends on what others then do. Kant's own variation makes the point: the friend may have slipped out, so that a lie sends the murderer to meet him (8:427). Michaelis had rejected harm-based definitions of the lie because "I can never be certain whether this or that untruth may not be very harmful to another" [@Timmermann2025, 169]. A duty so keyed can be applied only by forecasting the free choices of others, and so each speaker decides, case by case, whether the truth asked of him will harm someone. The clause is invariant in form, since a truth that harms others is a fixed type. It fails the third aspect of fixity, and fails the second through the third: those who deal with someone bound only by Constant's clause cannot count on what he says.

It also releases too much. A witness whose truthful testimony will convict the accused tells a truth that harms another, so by the clause the court has no right to it. Kettner and Annen pressed this objection, and Timmermann connects it with Kant's charge that Constant confused harming with wronging [@Timmermann2025, 100 n. 11]. Kant draws the distinction to deny that the truthful householder wrongs his friend: the harm is "merely a coincidence (*casus*)" (8:428). For Constant the same distinction locates his clause's mistake. It treats every truth that harms as if telling it wronged. A clause keyed to wrong, not harm, would leave the witness's duty intact; to exclude the witness otherwise, Constant would need an exception to his own intermediate principle.

So the 1797 resolution fails, by Constant's standards and for reasons he had given three years before. None of this shows that a duty restricted by reference to persons must be an exception. It shows that Constant needed a different key.

# Pretended laws {#sec-pretended}

Timmermann's denial that the case is about the state is right about 1797. The example is a stock one; a likely source, on Timmermann's reconstruction, is Schaumann's Kantian natural law of 1796, in which "someone in a fury" pursues an innocent man who is hiding in my house [@Timmermann2025, 46]. Constant made the pursuers plural "assassins" and the victim "your friend". In his pamphlet assassins are not agents of the state: the first chapter describes leaders of the reaction who incited their followers "to the assassination of their accomplices" and made "national vengeance illegal and atrocious" (6). Chapter VII fears that if the royalists triumphed "proscription would be without end and without limits" (50), and calls on the friends of liberty to defend men whom some would make "a proscribed and terrible race, which would have no asylum on earth but beneath the ruins of the social order", while rallying "to the government, when it moderates opinion" (56–57). In 1797 the republican government was, for Constant, the protector of the proscribed, not their pursuer.

But the next chapter, "De l'arbitraire", contains the materials for a key different from harm. Institutions exist only as they exist by right: "there is nothing existing in an institution but what exists by right" (85). A government that resorts to the arbitrary "gives the same rights that it takes"; when it tells a people its laws are insufficient, "all the legitimate authority of a government falls: only force remains to it; it is no longer a government" (86). "A people and a government are always in reciprocity of duties": if the government's relation to the people is in the law, the people's relation to the government will be in the law, but if it is in the arbitrary, "the relation of the people to the government will likewise be in the arbitrary" (86–87). And "the arbitrary offers individuals no asylum" (87). Here duties are again correlated with rights, as in chapter VIII, but what releases a person from them is not the consequence of performing them. It is the character of the claimant: power that has abandoned law has abandoned its claim.

In 1797 Constant did not apply this to truthfulness. In 1815 he did. Chapter XVII of the *Principes de politique* discusses Rousseau's civil profession of faith, whose articles the sovereign may fix and whose unbelievers he may banish as unsociable. A footnote reports Rousseau's addition, that whoever has publicly acknowledged the dogmas and behaves as if he did not believe them is to be punished with death, for "he has lied before the laws". Constant replies:

> But he who has the misfortune not to believe these dogmas cannot avow his doubts without exposing himself to banishment; and if his affections hold him back, if he has a family, a wife, children whom he hesitates to leave to rush into exile, is it not you, you alone, who force him to what you call the greatest of crimes, to lying before the laws? I will say, moreover, that in this circumstance this lie seems to me far from being a crime. *Quand de prétendues lois n'exigent de nous la vérité que pour nous proscrire, nous ne leur devons pas la vérité*: when pretended laws demand the truth of us only to proscribe us, we do not owe them the truth. [@Constant1872, 128–129 n. 1]^[I cite the 1815 text from Laboulaye's edition [@Constant1872], which reprints the *Principes* as the first part of the *Cours de politique constitutionnelle*; the note reads the same in a recent reprint of the 1815 text. I have not been able to check whether it already appears in the unpublished *Principes* of 1806.]

The main text goes on to say that a state which judges sentiments loses itself in "a hypothetical morality, no less subtle, no less foreign to its natural jurisdiction" (129), and the work's first chapter states the limit: sovereignty "exists only in a limited and relative way", and "at the point where independence and individual existence begin, the jurisdiction of this sovereignty stops" [@Constant1872, 9].

The note's case differs from the 1797 case in three ways. The truth demanded is about the speaker's own beliefs, not a fact about someone else; the one to be proscribed is the speaker himself; and the demand comes from something with the form of law, not from assassins. I know of no evidence that Constant had the 1797 exchange in mind. What the note shows is the shape of key his theory allowed. The duty is still owed, "nous ne leur devons pas", so the correlation of chapter VIII survives. But what defeats the claim to the truth is not the truth's effect. It is the demand: made by laws that are only "pretended", because they exceed the jurisdiction of law, and made "only to proscribe". The first condition is chapter IX's reciprocity applied to truthfulness. The second is a purpose, and the purpose is a wrong, not a harm.

At the door only the second condition has work to do. The assassins make no claim to law, and a legitimate authority might ask the same question. What disqualifies them is that they demand the truth only in order to do wrong. Read this way, the principle Constant's later work supplies for the 1797 case is: those who demand the truth only in order to wrong are not owed it. That is close to Timmermann's paraphrase, with "wrong" in place of "harm". His paraphrase describes the principle Constant came to better than the one he stated. The difference matters for the witness. The court's demand is neither pretended nor proscriptive, and the truth it asks for may harm the accused without wronging him, so the later principle leaves the witness's duty where it was. It must not be read as making title the only source of the right, as if "where there are no rights, there are no duties" released us from truthfulness towards anyone without official standing; on that reading the stranger asking the way would have no right to a true answer. The note's structure is a claim to the truth that is ordinarily owed and is defeated by two features of the demand.

Does the later key meet Constant's standard? It does better than the harm clause on the aspect of fixity that clause failed. Whether a demand comes from competent authority, and whether its purpose is proscription, are features of a present demand, judged by public criteria, not forecasts of what others will freely do. But purposes must be inferred, and whether a law is merely pretended is often what is in dispute. Constant knew this by 1815. In the chapter on subordinate agents who execute illegal orders, he holds that the limits of obedience "cannot be described, because it is impossible to foresee all the cases that may arise; but they are felt", and that each man "is judge of them, and necessarily the only judge … at his own risk and peril" [@Constant1872, 92]. What the agent must judge is title: whether an order "emanates from the authority that has the right to give it" and bears "the prescribed formalities", for "an innocent man may be arrested quite legally, if he is suspected" (92–93 n. 1). And Constant concedes: "there is uncertainty in all human things. To free himself from all uncertainty, man would have to cease to be a moral being" (93). In 1797 "each person is judge of the circumstances" described the arbitrary, and the right modification "excludes all arbitrariness and all uncertainty". In 1815 Constant gives up that aspiration. What remains of the arbitrary is to be checked by institutions, by juries who judge each case once and have no permanent interest in power, not by a further principle. At the door there is no jury. The later key is better than the earlier one, but by a weaker standard than the one Constant set in 1797, and one closer to Kant's insistence that applying rules requires judgement.

# What remains {#sec-remains}

Both of Constant's keys bear on the questioner's right, and that is the one point Kant concedes. "Although I do no wrong to him who unjustly compels me to a statement if I falsify it", I do wrong "in the most essential part of duty in general", making declarations in general unbelievable, "a wrong done to humanity in general" (8:426). The duty is owed "towards everyone" (8:426) and "makes no distinction between persons" (8:429). What Kant calls Constant's πρῶτον ψεῦδος, his fundamental error, is neither the harm clause nor any key, but the premise that "telling the truth is a duty, but only towards someone who has a right to the truth" (8:425). Timmermann argues that the juridical argument Kant built on it is weak and that Kant's absolutism really rests on the ethical duty to oneself [-@Timmermann2025, 156–157]. Either way, nothing about the questioner's standing reaches it. Constant improved his key between 1797 and 1815. He never gave up the correlation, and the correlation is what Kant denied.

The two men can be compared on a case both discussed. In *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason*, which Constant read in 1794 according to Kloocke [@Timmermann2025, 42], Kant asks whether spiritual superiors may require the people, "on pain of losing their station", to profess as articles of faith what they cannot know to be true. Such a superior "would himself act against conscience" and "must answer for all the misuse arising from such compulsory faith"; yet "there may be truth in what is believed, but at the same time untruthfulness in the believing (or even in its merely inner profession), and this is in itself damnable" (6:187). Sincerity, Kant adds, "must be demanded of every human being" (6:190 n.). Constant's note addresses the same kind of case. Like Kant, he blames the one who compels, "is it not you, you alone, who force him", but where Kant finds the untruthful profession damnable in itself, Constant finds it "far from being a crime". The difference is not about harm, consequences or exceptions, which neither invokes, and not about the compeller's guilt, on which they agree. It is about whether truthfulness is owed to the one who asks.

Centring Constant thus changes what the example is about. Read from Kant's side, it is a test of whether a strict duty yields to catastrophe. Read from Constant's, it is a test of what makes a principle fixed. His first answer failed by his own standard. His second, keyed to the legitimacy and purpose of the demand, meets it as well as any principle of application can, which by 1815 he thought was not perfectly. His view that duties of truthfulness are owed to persons who have a claim on them was constant from 1797 to 1815, and it is that view, not expediency, that Kant set out to refute.
